en: Without loosening its strap from his neck,
He drew it from his breast,
Displaying his valor,
And revealing himself as a true hero.
Any creature that saw him
Fled, despairing of life.
Atop Kulunsur,
He sat leaning to one side,
Filling his mind with resolve.
The noble hero, wolf of battle,
Did not flinch or care,
Considering suffering and doom—
Even certain death in the end—
Not worth the hem of his robe.
He turned the wheel
Of the telescope left by the magnanimous hero,
Set it firmly to his eye,
Turned its focusing screw,
And raised it to his eye.
He gazed across Keng-Özön’s expanse,
Toward the place where peris played,
To the marshland of wondrous delights,
Where moon-beautiful Akbermet,
The ill-fated peri-maiden,
Was swinging on a swing.
He stretched forward and stared.
Smoke drifted away in wisps;
Red tents and blue tents,
And bright, many-colored possessions—
Women’s belongings came into view.
Smoke rose and divided toward the sky,
And marvels of every kind appeared.
Anyone who looked carefully
Was left utterly bewildered.
There were wonders of myriad kinds,
And women’s belongings came into view.
Erected for an outing,
A white tent stood to the north.
When he examined that tent,
Its poles were gold and its ropes were brass;
Its like had never appeared in the world.
Unless it had come from the peris,
No mortal could have made such a thing.
Such was the breadth of that tent:
It was called a tent, but was a white palace—
The tale of the splendor
With which it was adorned is long indeed.
It was a single tent with one entrance,
Yet from the far side it seemed different;
Seen within, it was a thousand tents.
In one corner of the tent,
Grey-maned Seytek and Akjoltoy
Seemed to be playing ordo.
In another part of the tent,
Brave Seytek, seeker of the maiden,
Together with his thirteen warriors,
Could fit inside with horses and armor.
In another corner of the tent,
Beside Bermet, daughter of the peris,
There were eighty maidens,
And all seemed to fit with room to spare.
Seeing this, Akjoltoy
Could not help but rejoice.
At the entrance of the tent,
A guardian stood watching—
Ask not what sort of guardian.
He received his orders from Bermet,
And wherever she sent him,
He brought calamity.
He stood ready with an iron-headed club,
Wearing human noses and ears
Strung as amulets upon him.
Anyone who saw his appearance from afar
Was driven out of his senses.
The ill-fated peri-maiden
Had selected him from warriors of many kinds
And stationed him there in splendor.
The radiant, ill-fated maiden did this:
“If he is a hero favored by the spirits,
If he is a man worthy of his forefathers,
Let him pass among the champions
And strike down the guardian demon.
If he is one who does not take after his father,
Let him squander all his wealth,
Then panic and flee back.
If he is a dark grey-maned hero,
If he is a bloodthirsty warrior-sultan,
He will darken with rage
And charge among the champions.
He will throw everything into turmoil,
And leave the place desolate;
He will wreak slaughter and raise dust,
Attack like a leopard,
And strike them from the flank.
If he is a foolish coward,
He will panic, unable to think,
And flee toward his village.”
Thus she stationed a warrior among the champions as guard,
And set every peril in equal measure.
So wise was the radiant,
Ill-fated peri-maiden,
So profound was her judgment.
She sought to test whether the hero was worthy to marry,
To gauge his courage
And thus discover his lionhearted strength.
If Seytek proved base,
Far from marrying him, she would not even approach,
But would scatter all her possessions,
Transform herself by reciting a spell,
And flee toward the peris.
She pondered wisely,
Thinking deeply upon everything:
“If Seytek proves a hero,
Let us immerse ourselves in celebration,
Eat meat together from a single platter,
And meet face-to-face.
If he satisfies Seytek’s heart,
Let her follow him and die at his side.”
Guarding what she carried within,
To entrust her cherished charge.
To discern the hero’s valor and courage,
For Bermet to behold and know,
To satisfy her heart,
And only then to marry him.
The doubly ill-fated one,
A world as fleeting as the setting moon.
The wondrous, incorrigible one,
Wearying horses and ranging the land,
Running hounds and flying falcons,
“If he bears the mark of valor,
In the end he will come seeking me,” she said,
“If he comes seeking, he shall see,” she said,
“But if his heart is faint,
He will die before his destined hour,” she said,
“If he should die, Akbermet
Will then enjoy at least one day,” she said.
She gathered an extraordinary band of wrestlers,
And several mighty warriors;
Looking farther beyond them,
She had them stationed there by magic.
Her tigers had borne twins;
None who encountered them returned alive.
Her leopards had borne twins;
None who met them remained alive.
Her lions had borne twins;
None who faced them returned alive.
It was a place no human had ever entered,
No mortal creature walking on two feet.
Still farther on was another menace,
Another strange wonder stood there.
It had a sword-pointed tongue,
Which could cleave a mountain when it struck,
And lay a forest flat when it entered.
No traveler could pass that way;
Whoever met that ill-omened, monstrous beast
Could never remain alive.
Knowing this, Akjoltoy
Had set it there by magic.
Knowing its wickedness, Akjoltoy
Raged without a care:
“Whether fairy or giant,
In the end,” said wily Joltoy,
“I count it no more than the hem of my robe.”
Toward the gray hill where no living soul walked,
He turned Kulunsur’s head.
His silhouette loomed like a mountain,
And the hearts of those who saw him were shaken,
As he stood gazing at the maidens.
The splendid man, proud as a rooster,
The steadfast, lionhearted hero,
For the unfortunate fairy maiden,
For that radiant precious one,
Had journeyed far and crossed mountains,
And forded formidable, surging waters,
Coming in search of her, they said,
Leaving behind the fairies’ bazaar.
For the sake of hero Seytek,
She had sought to satisfy her longing.
Unable to reach the gray-maned hero,
She had camped along the Broad Valley.
Because of passion’s fire,
Many champions and countless armies
Had been crushed to dust upon the road.
“For this fierce woman who came seeking him,
Will he grant days of happiness?” they wondered.
“To Bermet, who has lived in this way,
What will hero Seytek do for her?” they wondered,
As he drove his spear into the ground.
Unable to collect his thoughts,
His anguish burning fiercely,
He turned toward the qibla
And wheeled Kulunsur around.
Marveling at this fleeting world,
Wily Joltoy stood watching.
The fairy maiden Akbermet
Was the youngest of six daughters;
Her pavilion was of white silk,
And but for being a woman,
She was the bravest of her sex.
When she reached eleven years of age,
Her father the sultan died.
When she reached thirteen,
She crossed through rain, hunted game,
And amused herself by drawing the bow.
When she reached fourteen,
Everything beneath the moon and sky
She comprehended through her wisdom.
When she reached fifteen,
She became the fairies’ sovereign khan,
And then Bermet ascended
Her father’s golden throne.
When she reached eighteen,
She reigned in royal splendor.
Her vast fairy host and numerous people
She ruled without letting them stir.
Her father, the sultan and padishah,
Had it built of precious stone:
A white palace fashioned of gold,
Fitted throughout with mirrors,
Stunning the hearts of all who saw it.
He had jewels piled there like kneeling camels,
And burning upon its braziers.
She entered it to sleep,
And when the hour of dawn approached,
All manner of things entered her dream;
While she lay troubled in sleep,
There appeared within her dream
A barefoot dervish.
The dervish stood and spoke,
Telling marvels no mortal had heard:
“Listen to my words:
You are the daughter of the radiant fairy,
The most skillful among women.
Understand what I tell you;
My child Akbermet, heed my counsel.
This is the destiny written by Allah;
Look closely at me,
And listen carefully to my words.
He is the rightful heir to truth,
The offspring of the true Kyrgyz;
His first forefather was Tümön Khan,
Blessed from the beginning by Khidr.
His earliest ancestors were all khans,
All of them blessed by Khidr.
Their fortune surged into a lake,
And from the first they were gray-maned lions.
When enemy warriors rose to fight them,
They were leveled with the black earth.
In the hearts of the Black Chinese and Manchus,
They became an incurable,
Deeply cutting pain.
His fathers and forefathers
Shattered royal camps and took their spoils,
And marched against the peoples of the world.

And enemies who dared attack
